nodes.bodyText:
New Feature Pitch
Often people write cool, super fast kernels that overlap with existing implementations in PyTorch. However PyTorch tensors can have a very large configuration space -> non-contiguous, nonzero offset, arbitrary dims, etc.. Often kernel authors are able to make their implementations so fast because they focus on a specific subset of the configuration space.
The pitch is that we should design a nice extension mechanism for people to "bring their own kernels" to PyTorch while also being able to fall back to PyTorch's base implementation for the cases their kernels don't support. I have coined this "intra kernel dispatching".
Rough Design
This would let users do something like
  dispatcher = AtenIntraKernelDispatcher()

  # Example 1: Override mm for small square matrices
  def is_small_square(self: torch.Tensor, mat2: torch.Tensor) -> bool:
      return (self.dim() == 2 and mat2.dim() == 2 and
              self.size(0) == self.size(1) == mat2.size(0) == mat2.size(1) <= 64)

  def custom_mm_kernel(self: torch.Tensor, mat2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
      print(f"[CUSTOM MM] {self.shape} @ {mat2.shape}")
      # Your optimized implementation here
      return torch.matmul(self, mat2)

  dispatcher.register("mm", is_small_square, custom_mm_kernel)

  print("Testing mm dispatch:")

  # Should use custom kernel
  print("\n1. Small square (32x32):")
  a = torch.randn(32, 32)
  b = torch.randn(32, 32)
  c = torch.mm(a, b)
This would allow users to build Libraries of external kernels, incrementally. They can be loaded to by PT users and git instant speedups. Similar ideas can be seen: https://github.com/FlagOpen/FlagGems
A Few existing Problems
I was looking at this with @albanD, there are a few problems today. The main one is once you override your op there is no nice way to get the original implementation. The implementation would check that there is a computed_key. If there is an existing compute key, then there is infact something to override. However we don't expose the ability today to get the KernelFunction for computed keys like we do for non computed keys.
We would then need to pybind kernelFunction's call boxed to use as the fall through in the dispatcher.
Besides all of the work above the other problem:
Libraries in PyTorch is responsible for the lifetime of the raw function pointer. Described in the mermaid doc below. It is possible to have
Lib1 -> Lib2 -> Lib3 where Lib3 stores a reference to a original_implementation that is based off a raw function in Lib2. If Lib2 gets destructed then raw_function has no owner and this can lead to use after free. Initial option is to check that previous Lib and or all of its dependencies are still alive before calling raw func

  
    
        graph TD
      Dispatcher --> |owns| OperatorHandle
      OperatorHandle --> |owns| OperatorEntry
      OperatorEntry --> |owns| KernelFunction

      CppLibrary[C++ Library manages lifetime] --> |owns raw function pointer| KernelFunction
      PythonLibrary[Python Library torch.library.py] --> |Python wrapper around| CppLibrary

      CppLibrary -.-> |deregistration can invalidate pointer| KernelFunction

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi there,
I’m reporting an issue where torch.export.export() fails on GPU when exporting a model that contains an nn.LSTMlayer. The same model exports successfully on CPU, which suggests a GPU-specific tracing or fake tensor handling issue. The error message references custom kernels, which seems unrelated to this model.
Minimal Reproduction Script
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SimpleLSTMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=10, hidden_size=20, num_layers=1):
        super(SimpleLSTMModel, self).__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers)
        self.linear = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        out, _ = self.lstm(x)
        out = self.linear(out)
        return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = SimpleLSTMModel()
    example_input = (torch.randn(5, 3, 10),)

    print("Attempting export on CPU...")
    try:
        model_cpu = model.to("cpu")
        exported_cpu = torch.export.export(model_cpu, example_input)
        print("CPU export succeeded.")
    except Exception as e:
        print("CPU export failed:", e)

    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        print("Attempting export on GPU...")
        try:
            model_gpu = model.to("cuda")
            input_gpu = (example_input[0].to("cuda"),)
            exported_gpu = torch.export.export(model_gpu, input_gpu)
            print("GPU export succeeded.")
        except Exception as e:
            print("GPU export failed:", e)
    else:
        print("GPU not available. Skipping GPU export.")
Output
Attempting export on CPU...
CPU export succeeded.
Attempting export on GPU...
GPU export failed: Cannot access data pointer of Tensor (e.g. FakeTensor, FunctionalTensor). If you're using torch.compile/export/fx, it is likely that we are erroneously tracing into a custom kernel. To fix this, please wrap the custom kernel into an opaque custom op. Please see the following for details: https://pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/custom_ops_landing_page.html


The error is likely caused by how torch.export interacts with GPU-backed LSTM internals. It's possible that torch.export is not properly handling fused GPU kernels or CUDNN ops when fake tensors are involved during graph capture.

Hi all, raising an issue to get an understanding of the state of ROCm 6.4.1 support in Pytorch.

nodes.title: nn.NLLLoss Fails with 1D Inputs in Compiled Mode

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
When compiling models using nn.Sequential with stateful execution (where each layer's input depends on the previous output), Dynamo corrupts convolution weight shapes during fake tensor simulation. This causes channel mismatch errors that don't occur in eager mode.
To Reproduce
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  

class Model(nn.Module):  
    def __init__(self):  
        super().__init__()  
        self.bottlenecks = nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # Correct shape: [128,64,3,3]  
            nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernel_size=1)              # Correct shape: [64,128,1,1]  
        )  
      
    def forward(self, x):  
        y = [x]  
        y.extend(m(y[-1]) for m in self.bottlenecks)  # Stateful execution  
        return y[-1]  

x = torch.randn(32, 64, 224, 224)  
model = Model()  
model(x)  # Eager mode works  
torch.compile(model, backend="eager")(x)  # Compiled mode fails

import torch

    @staticmethod

        attach_gradient = ctx.attach_gradient

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi,
I noticed a discrepancy in cuda graph capture for torch.fake_quantize_per_channel_affine between nvidia/AMD devices.
Running CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python debug_cuda_graph.py:
import torch

in_shape = 4096

inputs = torch.rand(in_shape, 1, device="cuda")
scale = torch.rand(in_shape, device="cuda").abs() + 0.5
zero_point = torch.randint(low=0, high=15, size=(in_shape,), dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
axis = 0
quant_min = 0
quant_max = 15

def fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(x, scales, zero_points):
    res = x
    for i in range(128):
        for j in range(1):
            res = torch.fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(res, scales, zero_points, axis, quant_min, quant_max)
            #res = 2 * res
    return res


g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()

# Warmup before capture
s = torch.cuda.Stream()
s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
with torch.cuda.stream(s):
    for _ in range(3):
        res = fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(inputs, scale, zero_point)
torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)

# Captures the graph
# To allow capture, automatically sets a side stream as the current stream in the context
with torch.cuda.graph(g):
    res = fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(inputs, scale, zero_point)

# Fills the graph's input memory with new data to compute on
inputs.copy_(torch.randn(in_shape, 1, device="cuda"))
g.replay()

inputs.copy_(torch.randn(in_shape, 1, device="cuda"))
g.replay()
on NVIDIA devices (H100) with torch==2.7.1+cu128 raises
  File "/vllm-workspace/debug_cuda.py", line 16, in fake_quantize_per_channel_affine
    res = torch.fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(res, scales, zero_points, axis, quant_min, quant_max)
          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
RuntimeError: CUDA error: operation not permitted when stream is capturing

Running on AMD devices (MI300), running the same code does give the error operation not permitted when stream is capturing.
Then, trying to capture with a larger loop count:
def fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(x, scales, zero_points):
    res = x
    for i in range(128):
        for j in range(100):
            res = torch.fake_quantize_per_channel_affine(res, scales, zero_points, axis, quant_min, quant_max)
    return res

errors out with Segmentation fault (core dumped). Smaller loop count does not segfault.
Is the difference in behavior between Nvidia/AMD devices expected? I would expect to have a https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/docs-6.4.1/reference/error_codes.html#term-hipErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported raised as well, in case the code path is the same between rocm/cuda for this operator.
Thank you!

🐛 Describe the bug
import torch
import torchvision


efficientnet = torchvision.models.efficientnet_b0(
    dropout=0.2, weights="IMAGENET1K_V1"
).to(device="cuda")
efficientnet_preprocess = efficientnet.features[0:6]

B = 32*100
x = torch.randn(B, 3, 192, 192).to(device="cuda")
x.requires_grad = False

compile = False

@torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
def forward_compiled(x):
    features = efficientnet_preprocess(x)
    return features

def forward(x):
    features = efficientnet_preprocess(x)
    return features

# no_grad just to save memory.
# errors with / without no_grad.
with torch.no_grad():
    if compile:
        # Will run fine
        print("Compiled forward starting")
        y = forward_compiled(x)
        print(y.sum())
        print("Compiled forward done")
    else:
        # Error
        # RuntimeError: Expected canUse32BitIndexMath(input) && canUse32BitIndexMath(output) to be true
        print("Eager forward starting")
        y = forward(x)
        print(y.sum())
        print("Eager forward done")

This code will work fine in compiled mode but in eager mode it will error on a convolution inside the efficientnet.
  File "/tmp/elefant-uv-env/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/conv.py", line 549, in _conv_forward
    return F.conv2d(
           ~~~~~~~~^
        input, weight, bias, self.stride, self.padding, self.dilation, self.groups
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    )
    ^
RuntimeError: Expected canUse32BitIndexMath(input) && canUse32BitIndexMath(output) to be true, but got false.  (Could this error message be improved?  If so, please report an enhancement request to PyTorch.)

What I would expect, pytorch should use 64 bit index in both eager and compiled in this case.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I’m integrating my device profiler with PyTorch’s profiler.
A run generates tons of tiny, low-level events. These events are helpful for later analysis, but they mess up the table produced by
profiler.key_averages().table()
Right now the only way to hide those events is inside the private function _parse_kineto_results(), which skips events by checking their names against a hard-coded list:
# torch/autograd/profiler.py
for kineto_event in result.events():
    if _filter_name(kineto_event.name()):
        ...
Keeping that ignore list up to date is fragile - whenever an event name changes, the filter fails and the table becomes noisy again.
Proposal
Add an optional hide flag to each event’s metadata.
If hide=True, PyTorch omits that event from the key_averages() table, so noisy low-level events disappear without the need for a long ignore list.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
No response
cc @robieta @chaekit @guotuofeng @guyang3532 @dzhulgakov @davidberard98 @briancoutinho @sraikund16 @sanrise

🐛 Describe the bug
On AMD GPUs, if there is a module containing a call to torchvision.transforms.v2.functionnal.resize on a torch.uint8 input, the output changes when using torch.compile on the module.
Running on a MI300 GPU with torch 2.7.0a0+git3a58512 and torchvision 0.19.1a0+6194369 (torch 2.7.0 failed to even compile so I had to pick the right commit), here is a minimal reproducible example:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torchvision.transforms.v2 import functional as F

class Resizer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, height: int, width: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.height = height
        self.width = width

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return F.resize(x, (self.height, self.width), interpolation=F.InterpolationMode.BICUBIC, antialias=True)

if __name__ == "__main__":

    x = torch.randn((3, 41, 70)).mul(256).to(torch.uint8).to("cuda:0")
    resizer = Resizer(384, 384)
    y = resizer(x)
    resizer = torch.compile(resizer)
    y_compiled = resizer(x)
    print(f"Max difference: {y.float().sub(y_compiled.float()).abs().max().item()}")

# stdout: Max difference: 255.0

I think it has something to do with the graph made by torch.compile, here is a gist where the issue is fixed: https://gist.github.com/remi-or/eb8936ca093d54c186fb5b67f15334eb
If I use torch.clamp instead of the two masked_fll the issue is still there, might be related.

🐛 Describe the bug
torch.compile failed in all_to_all_single_grad when passing dynamic input/output splits.
all_to_all_single_grad is introduced by #123599 and claimed to be working with torch.compile.
A minimal reproducer:
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import all_to_all_single_autograd

torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True
torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True
torch.manual_seed(0)
world_size = 2
num_experts = 4
mesh = dist.init_device_mesh("cuda", (world_size, ))
rank = dist.get_rank()
device = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}")
group = mesh.get_group()

compile = True

def my_func(x: torch.Tensor, num_local_tokens_per_expert: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:

    with torch.no_grad():
        tokens_per_expert_group = num_local_tokens_per_expert.new_empty(
            num_local_tokens_per_expert.shape[0])
        dist.all_to_all_single(tokens_per_expert_group,
                               num_local_tokens_per_expert,
                               group=group)
        input_splits = num_local_tokens_per_expert.view(world_size, -1).sum(dim=1)
        output_splits = tokens_per_expert_group.view(world_size, -1).sum(dim=1)
    gathered_tokens = all_to_all_single_autograd(
        x,
        output_splits.tolist(),
        input_splits.tolist(),
        group,
    )

    return gathered_tokens

compiled_fn = torch.compile(my_func, fullgraph=True) if compile else my_func

num_local_tokens_per_expert = torch.arange(
    num_experts, device=device, dtype=torch.int32) + 1
x = torch.randn((num_local_tokens_per_expert.sum().item(), 2), device=device, requires_grad=True)
out = compiled_fn(x, num_local_tokens_per_expert)
loss = out.sum()
loss.backward()

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
I’d like to report what appears to be an inconsistent behavior when using torch.export.export() on models with empty forward methods, especially those involving variadic arguments (*args, **kwargs). While such models are likely ill-defined for production use, the difference in export behavior and the cryptic error message suggest there might be an issue in how the input arguments are handled internally.
Reproduction Script
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import os
os.environ["TORCH_LOGS"] = "+dynamo"
os.environ["TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE"] = "1"

class EmptyForwardModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x, *args, **kwargs):
        pass

class EmptyForwardModel_1(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        pass
model = EmptyForwardModel()
model_1 = EmptyForwardModel_1()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    example_input = (torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224),)
    try:
        output = model(example_input)
        print(f"output is {output}")
    except Exception as e:
        print("model output error: ", str(e))
    try:
        exported_model = torch.export.export(model, example_input)
        print("Exported model is exported successfully.")
    except Exception as e:
        print("[EXPORT FAILED]: model ", e)
    try:
        output_1 = model_1(example_input)
        print(f"output_1 is {output_1}")
        exported_model_1 = torch.export.export(model_1, example_input)
        print("Exported model_1 is exported successfully.")
    except Exception as e:
        print("[EXPORT FAILED]: model_1 ", e)
Observed Output
output is None
[EXPORT FAILED]: model  list index out of range
output_1 is None
Exported model_1 is exported successfully.

Problem Summary


EmptyForwardModel (with *args, **kwargs) fails to export with a cryptic error: list index out of range


EmptyForwardModel_1 (without *args, **kwargs) successfully exports, even though its forward also returns None


I suspect the error may stem from the way torch.export processes *args and **kwargs—possibly during input flattening or argument binding. It seems like the internal tracing expects a fixed number of inputs and fails to handle *args correctly when the forward does nothing.

import torch

@torch.compile(dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)
def test_compile(x: torch.Tensor, dim: Sequence[int] = ()) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Use the first dimension if dim is empty, otherwise use the specified dimensions
    reduction_dims = list(dim) if dim else [0]
    
    first_dim = reduction_dims[0]

Abstract
This PEP proposes an evolution of Python Wheels standard to support hardware-specific or platform-dependent package variants. Current mechanisms for distinguishing Python Wheels (i.e Python ABI version, OS, CPU architecture, and Build ID) are insufficient for modern hardware diversity, particularly for environments requiring specialized dependencies such as high performance computing, hardware accelerated software (GPU, FPGA, ASIC, etc.), etc.
This proposal introduces Wheel Variants, a mechanism for publishing platform-dependent wheels and selecting the most suitable package variant for a given platform.
To enable fine-grained package selection without fragmenting the Python ecosystem, this PEP proposes:
A Wheel Variant system that enables multiple wheels for the same Python package version, distinguished by hardware-specific attributes.
A Provider Plugin system that dynamically detects platform attributes and recommends the most suitable wheel.
A hash-based identification mechanism for wheel variants, ensuring compatibility while maintaining clarity in package naming.
This approach allows seamless package resolution without requiring intrusive changes to installers, ensures backward compatibility, and minimizes the burden on package maintainers.

import timm, torch

🐛 Describe the bug
I would like to report an issue I encountered when trying to export a scripted model that returns a dictionary (Dict[str, Tensor]) using torch.onnx.export. The behavior appears inconsistent between traced and scripted models, and the error messages are currently not very user-friendly.
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.onnx
from typing import Dict

class DictOutputModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
        return {'output': x}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = DictOutputModel()
    model.eval()

    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
    jit_model = torch.jit.script(model)

    for i in range(7, 20):
        try:
            torch.onnx.export(
                jit_model,
                dummy_input,
                f="jit_model.onnx",
                opset_version=i,
            )
            print(f"ONNX jit_model exported successfully")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] ONNX jit_model export failed: {e}")

        try:
            torch.onnx.export(
                model,
                dummy_input,
                f="model.onnx",
                opset_version=i
            )
            print(f"ONNX model exported successfully")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] ONNX model export failed: {e}")

The raw nn.Module with a Dict[str, Tensor] output is exportable.
The same model after torch.jit.script fails to export via torch.onnx.export, regardless of the opset version.
The output is like:

ONNX model exported successfully
Torch IR graph at exception: graph(%x.1 : Float(1, 3, 224, 224, strides=[150528, 50176, 224, 1], requires_grad=0, device=cpu)):
  %2 : str = prim::Constant[value="output"](), scope: DictOutputModel:: # /data/zyzhao/DLframework/run_module/minimal_script/test_coverage/model1.py:8:16
  %3 : Dict(str, Tensor) = prim::DictConstruct(%2, %x.1), scope: DictOutputModel::
  return (%3)

[ERROR] ONNX jit_model export failed: Exporting the operator 'prim::DictConstruct' to ONNX opset version 17 is not supported. Please feel free to request support or submit a pull request on PyTorch GitHub: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues.


From previous issues and docs, I noticed that setting dynamo=True may resolve this for higher opset versions. However, for lower opsets (e.g., <18), I see output like:

[torch.onnx] Obtain model graph for `RecursiveScriptModule(original_name=DictOutputModel)` with `torch.export.export(..., strict=False)`...

Concern

🐛 Describe the bug
I came across this segfault while writing some tests, and @StrongerXi has reproduced:
import torch

def random_tensor(size, dtype, **kwargs):
    if dtype in [torch.half, torch.bfloat16, torch.float, torch.double]:
        return torch.randn(size, dtype=dtype, **kwargs)
    elif dtype in [torch.uint8, torch.int8, torch.short, torch.int, torch.long]:
        return torch.randint(0, 100, size, dtype=dtype, **kwargs)
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported data type")

def cT(device, dtype):
    def T(*shape, requires_grad=False):
        return random_tensor(
            shape, requires_grad=requires_grad, device=device, dtype=dtype
        )

    return T

def pointwise_test_model(device, dtype, compile=True):
    T = cT(device, dtype)
    def model():
        M = 256
        N = 512
        mat3 = T(M, N)
        mat4 = T(M, N)
        pointwise_output = torch.add(mat3, mat4).sin()
        return pointwise_output
    return model

device = "cuda"
dtype = torch.float16
om = pointwise_test_model(device, dtype, compile=False)
print("compile 1")
comp_omni = torch.compile(om)

# print("run 1")
# comp_omni()

print("reset 1")
torch._dynamo.reset()

print("run 2")
comp_omni()

print("compile 2")
comp_omni = torch.compile(om)

print("run 3")
comp_omni()

📚 The doc issue
On the docs for amin/amax there's a note that describes the difference between amin/amax and min/max:
amax/amin evenly distributes gradient between equal values, while max(dim)/min(dim) propagates gradient only to a single index in the source tensor.

This is outdated - the behavior of min/max was changed in #43519
Suggest a potential alternative/fix

nodes.title: ROCm: torch.cholesky_inverse raises Memory access fault for large tensor shapes

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The rocm build of torch 2.7 (and 2.5.1, and possible others) allows for indexing beyond the bounds of arrays when indexing with an iterable for tensors placed on the GPU:
import torch
a = torch.tensor([1,2,3,4])
b = torch.tensor([1,2,3,4], device='cuda:0')

a[4] # Errors out
b[4] # Errors out

a[[4, 4]] # Errors out
b[[4, 4]] # Runs
Will also allow us to write, not just read:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([1], device='cuda:0')
b = torch.tensor([2], device='cuda:0')

# Ensure sequential blocks
mem_info_0 = torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()[0]['blocks'][0]
mem_info_1 = torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()[0]['blocks'][1]
block_size = mem_info_0['size']
address_0_w_offset = mem_info_0['address'] + block_size
address_1 = mem_info_1['address']
assert address_0_w_offset == address_1, "Memory blocks are not sequential"
 
a[[block_size // 8]] = 99 # // 8 to convert from blocksize to element index

assert b == 2, "Modified tensor b through out of bounds access"
Versions
2.7+rocm6.3 and 2.5.1+rocm6.2. Possibly others

nodes.title: Indexing beyond end of array on ROCm build

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
input dim > 2 seems to result in CPU setting grad to all zeros, even for trivial "unsqueeze" style shape padding
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

dtype = torch.float
device = 'cuda'
logits = torch.randn(5, 1, 24, dtype=dtype, device=device, requires_grad=True)
out = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)
grad = torch.randn_like(out)
out.backward(grad)
logits_cpu = logits.detach().cpu()
logits_cpu.requires_grad = True
out_cpu = F.log_softmax(logits_cpu, dim=1)
out_cpu.backward(grad.detach().cpu())
torch.testing.assert_close(out, out.cuda())
print(logits.grad, logits_cpu.grad)
torch.testing.assert_close(logits.grad, logits_cpu.grad.cuda())

🐛 Describe the bug
I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
import torch
torch.random.manual_seed(42)
from torch import nn

dtype = torch.float16
batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
x2 = x1[:, delay:]
assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
out1 = net(x1)
out2 = net(x2)
print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
I got the output like this:
tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
    assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
AssertionError

If the type is bfloat16, the error is even greater:
tensor(0.0078, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.bfloat16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
    assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
AssertionError

However, if the tensor is cloned after sliced x2 = x1[:, delay:].clone() or the type is float32, it will produce an error of exactly zero.
tensor(0., device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)

I don't know if this is an allowable margin of error or a bug.

🐛 Describe the bug
This is a strange issue only observed locally on AMD/ROCm runs, when torch.compiling a simple dynamic shapes conv2d+batchnorm2d example. Without dynamic shapes this passes fine. Looking at the codegen, it generates (1/3)*x0 in the tl.load, resulting in a float output which fails the the tl.load. Replacing this with integer divison the triton code at least compiles and executes.
Reproducer:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SimpleBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width_in, width_out=224, stride=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(width_in, width_out, kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False)
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(width_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv(x)
        x = self.bn(x)
        return x

test_cases = [
    ((2, 32, 470, 725), 32),
    ((2, 224, 235, 363), 224),
]

for input_shape, width_in in test_cases:
    model = SimpleBlock(width_in).train().to(dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cuda')
    input_tensor = torch.randn(*input_shape, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cuda')
    model = torch.compile(model)
    output = model(input_tensor)
